params.question: Every child presenting with acute suppurative otitis media should receive a CT scan of the temporal bone to rule out mastoiditis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: ASOM is diagnosed clinically and treated with antibiotics. Routine CT is unjustified because it adds radiation without changing the plan. Imaging is warranted only when red flags (post-auricular swelling, facial droop, vertigo, altered consciousness) suggest complications beyond the middle-ear cleft.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Exactly right. Uncomplicated ASOM is a clinical diagnosis treated with antibiotics. CT adds radiation without changing management. Imaging is reserved for red flags — post-auricular swelling, facial palsy, vertigo, or altered consciousness — indicating infection has spread beyond the middle-ear cleft.

params.question: A patient who underwent mastoid surgery for cholesteatoma two years ago requires surveillance imaging to detect possible recurrence. Which modality is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plain mastoid radiographs are obsolete. They cannot resolve the scutum, ossicles, or fine canal structures required for post-operative assessment.
HRCT maps bone detail exquisitely but cannot distinguish cholesteatoma from granulation tissue or fluid — all appear as identical soft-tissue opacity.

Correct. Non-EPI DWI detects cholesteatoma because its packed keratin restricts water diffusion, appearing bright on DWI. Granulation tissue does not restrict. This is the modality of choice for detecting recurrence without re-opening the ear.
Contrast-enhanced CT slightly improves soft-tissue visualisation but still cannot reliably distinguish cholesteatoma from granulation tissue.

overallFeedback.feedback: HRCT is the workhorse for bone anatomy, but it cannot differentiate soft tissues. Non-echo-planar DWI-MRI detects cholesteatoma recurrence by exploiting its diffusion restriction, without re-opening the ear.
Non-EPI DWI-MRI is the modality of choice for post-surgical cholesteatoma surveillance — cholesteatoma restricts diffusion and appears bright, while granulation tissue does not.

params.question: A temporal bone CT in a patient with cholesteatomatous CSOM reveals erosion of the tegmen tympani with a small epidural collection. What is the most immediate clinical implication?

answers.text: The patient should be scheduled for elective canal-wall-up mastoidectomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Canal-wall-up mastoidectomy is considered for limited cholesteatoma with an intact posterior canal wall. Tegmen erosion with intracranial extension demands far more urgent intervention.

answers.text: The case converts from elective to a surgical emergency requiring neurosurgical backup

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tegmen erosion with an intracranial collection is life-threatening. The timeline compresses, neurosurgical backup enters the plan, and the case becomes an emergency.

answers.text: A repeat scan should be obtained in 6 weeks to assess progression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying when intracranial spread is demonstrated risks meningitis, brain abscess, or death. Interval scanning is inappropriate here.

answers.text: Medical management with intravenous antibiotics alone should be trialled first

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An established intracranial collection from cholesteatoma requires surgical evacuation. Antibiotics alone are insufficient when there is frank intracranial extension.

overallFeedback.feedback: When imaging shows tegmen erosion or an intracranial collection, the case is no longer elective. The timeline compresses, neurosurgical backup is required, and urgent surgical intervention is mandatory.
Tegmen erosion with intracranial extension converts an elective case to a surgical emergency — the finding directly changes the decision, timeline, and team involved.

params.question: On gadolinium-enhanced MRI, an avidly enhancing mass centred on the internal auditory meatus extends into the cerebellopontine angle with an 'ice-cream cone' shape. Which feature most reliably distinguishes this lesion from a meningioma in the same region?

answers.text: The schwannoma shows a dural tail sign

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The dural tail sign is associated with meningioma, not schwannoma. It represents thickened enhancing dura adjacent to the tumour.

answers.text: The schwannoma does not enhance after gadolinium administration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vestibular schwannoma enhances avidly on gadolinium MRI. A non-enhancing CPA lesion would suggest an epidermoid cyst instead.
Meningioma does not characteristically restrict on DWI. Diffusion restriction in the CPA is a feature of epidermoid cysts, not meningiomas.

answers.text: The meningioma is centred on the dura rather than the internal auditory meatus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Both schwannoma and meningioma enhance avidly. The distinguishing feature is location: schwannoma is centred on the IAM (ice-cream cone), while meningioma is centred on the dura of the posterior fossa.

overallFeedback.feedback: Both vestibular schwannoma and meningioma enhance on gadolinium MRI. The distinguishing feature is the centre of the mass: schwannoma arises from the IAM (forming the ice-cream cone), while meningioma is based on the dura of the posterior fossa.
Location is the key discriminator: vestibular schwannoma is centred on the IAM while meningioma is dural-based — both enhance avidly on gadolinium MRI, so enhancement alone does not distinguish them.

params.question: A 55-year-old presents with six months of progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and poor speech discrimination scores. Which imaging study should be ordered first?

answers.text: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Progressive unilateral SNHL with poor speech discrimination is a red flag for a retrocochlear lesion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the IAM and cerebellopontine angle is the modality of choice to detect vestibular schwannoma.

HRCT is the first investigation for chronic otitis media and bony pathology. For suspected retrocochlear pathology causing SNHL, MRI is the modality of choice because it images soft tissues along the auditory pathway.
Non-contrast brain CT has poor sensitivity for small CPA lesions and does not adequately visualise the internal auditory canal. It would miss an early vestibular schwannoma.
Plain mastoid radiographs are obsolete. They cannot resolve the internal auditory canal or CPA and provide no useful information for sensorineural hearing loss evaluation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Asymmetric or unilateral SNHL is a red flag for a retrocochlear lesion such as vestibular schwannoma. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice because it images the soft tissues of the IAM and CPA with high sensitivity.
Progressive unilateral SNHL with poor speech discrimination warrants gadolinium-enhanced MRI to exclude vestibular schwannoma — the modality matches the tissue question.
